subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch
description: One-minute skill: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch.

hook.text: There's a swirling mass of trash in the Pacific Ocean twice the size of Texas.

buildup.text: Ocean currents trap floating debris in a rotating gyre between Hawaii and California.

discovery.text: Most of the patch isn't visible. It's a soup of tiny fragments suspended just below the surface.

twist.text: There are five major garbage patches on Earth — one in every ocean basin.

climax.text: Cleanup ships exist, but the plastic flows in faster than any technology can remove it.

punchline.text: The ocean doesn't have a trash problem. We do. It just catches ours.

quiz.question: How many major garbage patches exist in the world's oceans?

details.summary: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is a massive accumulation of plastic debris in the North Pacific, covering an area roughly three times the size of France. It consists mostly of microplastics suspended in the water column rather than a visible island, making cleanup extremely challenging.
details.whyItMatters: The garbage patch symbolizes the global plastic pollution crisis. Its existence demonstrates how ocean currents concentrate waste from every continent into persistent marine debris zones.
takeaways: The patch covers about 1.6 million square kilometers
It consists mostly of tiny microplastics, not visible debris
Ocean currents trap and concentrate floating plastic waste

faq.question: Can the Great Pacific Garbage Patch be cleaned up?
faq.answer: Organizations like The Ocean Cleanup are deploying floating barriers to collect surface debris. However, the vast scale and predominance of microplastics make complete removal nearly impossible. Preventing plastic from entering the ocean in the first place is far more effective.

faq.question: Are there other garbage patches in the ocean?
faq.answer: Yes. Ocean gyres in the North Atlantic, South Pacific, South Atlantic, and Indian Ocean all have accumulated plastic debris zones. Every ocean basin has one, though the North Pacific patch is the largest and most studied.
